About

I'm a junior at UT Austin studying chemical engineering with a minor in economics. Most of my work lives in one of two places: keeping industrial processes compliant and running (Valero), or making composite materials do what the simulation says they should (Longhorn Racing, Röchling). The thread between them is automation. I'd rather build the tool that does the calculation than redo the calculation.

This year that's meant rebuilding a refinery's Title V emissions engine, running FEA on a Formula-style undertray, and spending a summer proving that a simulation-driven testing workflow could replace a fully physical one. All detailed below.

Valero Energy Corporation

Environmental Engineering Intern
Ardmore Refinery, OK · May 2026 – Present

Four parallel workstreams this rotation: replacing a failed emissions flowmeter, rebuilding the Title V reporting engine, evaluating a $1.65M wastewater capital project, and building automated health monitoring for critical instruments.

COMPLIANCE VCU Flow Meter Replacement

ProblemThe Vapor Combustor Unit destroys emissions from the gasoline loading rack, and its output is measured, not estimated, via a natural gas flowmeter. That flowmeter failed, forcing the site to estimate GHG emissions instead of measuring them directly: a real compliance gap.

ApproachEvaluated DP vs. Coriolis replacement options against the refinery's Approved Manufacturer List and the ±5% calibration tolerance required under 40 CFR 98.3(i)(2), while working around aging piping that couldn't be disrupted during install.

Candidate Coriolis flow meter evaluated for AML compliance
STATUS: Flowmeter path selected; coordinating install timeline with the Reliability group and drafting the MOC/work order.
REPORTING Title V "ATLAS" Emissions Engine

ProblemTitle V emissions ran through Excel models that were slow and hard to maintain. ATLAS, the plant's official system, was accurate but required specialized training and calculated in hour-based time steps instead of minutes; neither tool balanced usability with efficiency alone.

ApproachBuilt a hybrid Excel engine that replicates ATLAS's calculation logic with dynamic, minute-level time inputs organized by Emissions Unit Group, validated line-by-line against ATLAS output with an automatic root-cause loop for anything outside tolerance.

Target: ATLAS accuracy, Excel flexibility
RESULT: Produces consistent, audit-ready output without ATLAS training overhead. Currently extending validation to EUGs 9–13, the most time-intensive groups.
CAPITAL PROJECT Influent Lift Station: Golder Study Analysis

ProblemThe Influent Lift Station is critical to wastewater system performance. Oily sludge buildup was cutting into usable capacity and raising overflow risk: a direct regulatory exposure, since an overflow counts against the refinery's 6 Mg/year benzene limit under BWON (40 CFR Part 63, Subpart FF). Prior studies (Golder '12/'14, Caldwell '13) recommended over $1.65M in capital upgrades: a new pump and additional storage.

ApproachBuilt a root-cause framework (investigate pump performance, align Reliability against Operations, confirm the true root cause), then scored four remediation paths (chopper-pump retrofit, routine maintenance, chemical cleaning, a new engineering study) on cost, effectiveness, and risk.

Root-cause → short-term → long-term decision framework
Options scored on cost, effectiveness, and risk
RESULT: Authored the technical/economic proposal recommending a Vaughan chopper-pump retrofit as the primary fix, addressing the root cause directly, without waiting on the full $1.65M capital plan.
RELIABILITY Instrument Health Monitoring (SPC)

ProblemCritical environmental instruments can drift out of calibration silently between scheduled checks; by the time it's caught manually, it may already be a compliance issue.

ApproachBuilt SPC-based monitoring that calculates mean, standard deviation, and 2σ/3σ control limits per analyzer, tracks drift, variability, and step-changes, then assigns an automatic RED / YELLOW / GREEN status.

Weekly health matrix with a prioritized queue for Reliability
RESULT: Surfaces at-risk instruments, like an analyzer sitting in YELLOW for two straight weeks, before they become compliance incidents.

R&D Case Study

Röchling Industrial Composites · Research & Development Intern · Cleveland, OH · May – August 2025

Capstone Project: Simulation-Driven Composite Testing
JUN – AUG 2025

Status quo

100% of material testing was physical, with no simulation feeding the workflow: expensive in labor and materials, and reliant on trial-and-error that made early-stage design hard to optimize.

Proposed solution

Integrate ANSYS simulation into the loop to digitally test mechanical and thermal properties before committing to physical builds, a hybrid cycle where simulation guides testing and test results refine the simulation.

Why a Drag Reduction System (DRS) wing: DRS is a movable rear-wing flap used in motorsport to cut aerodynamic drag at speed. It sees rapid actuation, high-speed airflow, and transient thermal/mechanical loading: a real, bounded case study with clear performance targets and relevance to both racing and aerospace composite design.
PHASE 1Calculations & CAD

Modeled a simplified DRS rear wing in Onshape (main flap, movable flap, and structural supports) based on an inverted NACA 2408 airfoil for realistic aerodynamic behavior. Goal: increase velocity 10–12 km/h.

Drag force (0.5·ρ·v²·Cd·A) gave the closed-vs-open force differential; dividing by the flap's cross-section gave the operating stress. Thermal load was estimated as force × distance and checked against the resin's curing enthalpy to confirm thermal stability.

  • Net force (open → closed)21.14 N
  • Operating stress (open)3,675 Pa
  • Main / movable flap depth15.7″ / 13.7″
NACA 2408 profile basis; CAD renders, closed and open
PHASE 2Resin Formulation

Back-calculated the required resin properties from the mechanical/thermal targets: curing enthalpy between 12–85 J/g and operational stress resistance above 3,500 Pa. The initial resin (UTR 5149474) showed thermal resistance defects; resolved by reformulating with 2 PHR envirospheres.

Exact formulation is proprietary to Röchling and omitted here.

PHASE 3Physical Testing

Measured the directional mechanical properties ANSYS needs to simulate the composite realistically under load: stiffness, transverse coupling, and torsional/shear response, plus the thermal inputs for coupled thermal-structural analysis.

  • Young's Modulusstiffness, per axis
  • Poisson's Ratioaxial ↔ transverse coupling
  • Shear Modulustorsional / shear response
  • Thermal expansion (THB)α = 0.335 μm/m·°C
  • Cure validation (DSC)confirmed full cure
PHASE 4ANSYS Simulation

Structural: static simulation with orthotropic stiffness inputs to reflect the composite's anisotropic behavior. Converged cleanly, with maximum deformation appearing near the top core, especially under open-DRS loading, flagging where reinforcement matters most.

Structural FEA: deformation under load

Thermal: transient analysis using measured conductivity and expansion coefficients to trace heat flow and temperature distribution over time, coupled back into the structural model for a real-world performance read.

Thermal FEA: heat flow and gradient-induced strain
RESULT & BUSINESS CASE

The simulation converged within failure limits on the first run, with no re-meshing or boundary-condition rework needed, validating the hybrid workflow this project set out to test. Rolled into the broader Q3 initiative, the simulation-first approach saved an estimated 105 hours and $25,000 versus a fully physical validation cycle.

ANSYS licensing runs from ~$22K for entry-level Mechanical packages up to Enterprise tiers with HPC add-ons, with volume and academic discounts available, and its AI-assisted Engineering Copilot meaningfully shortens the training curve for new users.
